<a id="pm-s2"></a>
## 2. Definitions, validity and bounds

- **End-of-Line instance and solution** ([source](#stmt-def-eol)): An instance $I$ consists of two explicitly listed, acyclic, bounded-fanin Boolean circuits $$S,P:\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,\qquad n\geq1,$$ using AND, OR, and NOT gates, with unrestricted fan-out, and satisfying $$P(0^n)=0^n,\qquad S(0^n)\ne0^n,\qquad P(S(0^n))=0^n.$$ A solution is a string $v\ne0^n$ such that $$\label{eq:end-of-line-solution} P(S(v))\ne v\quad\text{or}\quad S(P(v))\ne v.$$ The input length $N\geq2$ includes the complete descriptions of both circuits and their input and output lists.
- **Generalized circuit and acceptable assignment** ([source](#stmt-def-gcircuit)): A generalized circuit $G=(V,T)$ has an explicitly listed finite set of nodes $V$ and a nonempty set of gates $T$. Each gate has one output and at most two inputs. A node is the output of at most one gate. Directed cycles and unrestricted fan-out are permitted. Every gate parameter $\alpha$ is a binary-encoded rational in $[0,1]$. For an assignment $x:V\to[0,1]$, write $x_a,x_b$ for input values and $x_z$ for the output. The five arithmetic gate types are $\varepsilon$-satisfied when the corresponding condition holds: $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Constant}(\alpha;z)&:&\quad \lvert x_z-\alpha\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\ \mathrm{Scale}(\alpha;a;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\alpha x_a\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\ \mathrm{Copy}(a;z)&:& \lvert x_z-x_a\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\ \mathrm{Add}(a,b;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\min\{x_a+x_b,1\}\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\ \mathrm{Subtract}(a,b;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\max\{x_a-x_b,0\}\rvert&\leq\varepsilon. \end{aligned}$$ The comparison gate $\mathrm{Less}(a,b;z)$ has the two implications $$x_a<x_b-\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ x_z\geq1-\varepsilon, \qquad x_a>x_b+\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ x_z\leq\varepsilon.$$ The Boolean gates have the following implications: $$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Or}(a,b;z):\qquad (x_a\geq1-\varepsilon\ \text{or}\ x_b\geq1-\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\ (x_a\leq\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ x_b\leq\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon;\\[2pt] \mathrm{And}(a,b;z):\qquad (x_a\geq1-\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ x_b\geq1-\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\ (x_a\leq\varepsilon\ \text{or}\ x_b\leq\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon;\\[2pt] \mathrm{Not}(a;z):\qquad x_a\leq\varepsilon&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\ x_a\geq1-\varepsilon&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon. \end{aligned}$$ For these four gate types, every applicable implication must hold. If no antecedent holds, any output in $[0,1]$ is permitted. In particular, the comparison thresholds are strict and the Boolean thresholds are weak. Let $M$ be the complete binary encoding length of $G$. For fixed $\varepsilon,\delta>0$ and a fixed polynomial $p$, an acceptable assignment is rational, has total binary encoding length at most $p(M)$, and $\varepsilon$-satisfies at least $(1-\delta)\|T\|$ gates. Each gate has equal weight; at most $\lfloor\delta\|T\|\rfloor$ gates may fail. Failed gates may violate their relations arbitrarily, but all their nodes still have one globally consistent value in $[0,1]$.
- **Computed forward and reconstruction prefixes** ([source](#stmt-macro-prefixes)): A *forward prefix of length $k$ with parameter $y$* has the first $k$ positions in $\pi_{\mathrm f}$ occupied. At occupied positions it obeys these rules: $S$ inputs copy the corresponding bits of $y$; $P$ inputs copy the corresponding designated $S$ outputs; every gate obeys its Boolean or copy rule; and dummies are zero. In addition, each occupied designated $P$ output equals the corresponding bit of $y$. Unoccupied contents are zero. A *reconstruction prefix of length $k$ from $y$* uses $\pi_{\mathrm r}$. Its occupied $P$ inputs copy $y$, its occupied $S$ inputs copy the designated $P$ outputs, and its occupied gates and dummies obey the same rules as above. Each occupied designated $S$ output must additionally equal the corresponding bit of $y$. Unoccupied contents are again zero.
- **Certified full operation** ([source](#stmt-op-full-operation)): A full operation specifies parent full slots, a target encoder $E_{\mathrm{out}}$, and a local expression $X^{st}_k(i,j)$ in the parents. For arbitrary exact duplicated full parents, $X$ must have duplicated systematic payload $v$ and satisfy an allowed A-axis constraint system. In addition, either its A system is that of the target, or $X$ satisfies the target’s B system. The required target is $E_{\mathrm{out}}v$. Scalar coefficients in linear combinations are identical at every index. They may depend on an identical clock and on previously certified, completed public address data. The specified covariant primitive $W(k)\mapsto W(k)\rho_e(k)$ below may additionally use its explicit index-dependent public matrix; it must satisfy the same axis-constraint requirements on $X$.
- **Extended inner graph** ([source](#stmt-ia-extended-path)): An extended label is $(c,b,\eta,t)$, where $c\in C$, $\eta\in\{0,1\}$, and $0\le t\le q-1$. In pre mode $\eta=0$, $b$ must be valid at stage $c$; in post mode $\eta=1$, it must be valid at stage $\gamma c$. Edges are the following: 1. in pre mode, increase $t$ by one until $q-1$; 2. at full pre progress, perform the enabled macro edit and change to post mode, retaining the frame and full progress; 3. in post mode, decrease $t$ by one until zero; 4. at empty post progress, change to empty pre mode in frame $\gamma c$, leaving $b$ unchanged. The fourth operation is included also for $c=\gamma^{-1}$; only the second operation is disabled at that frame.
- **Admissible local access** ([source](#stmt-geo-access-finite)): An *oracle access implementation* satisfies parts (a)–(c) below and the following operational condition. At its declared oracle level, each supplied bit or decision routine uses a bounded tree of completed Boolean answers, apart from public index computations. Every input, including an input outside a correctness promise, gives Boolean answers or public defaults. After its requested accuracies are fixed, the oracle tree and its symbolic query roles are bounded independently of $m$ and remain fixed under refinement of threshold-offset grids. These conditions impose no constant bound on the physical circuit realizing a completed oracle answer. Part (d) is an additional *physical-read hypothesis*, required only when a conclusion about the fully expanded physical reads is explicitly invoked. All constants are uniform in $m$, $X$, and admissible fixed offsets. Geometric and validation radii and the reference rule below are fixed before reliability and numerical accuracy choices. Operational, sample, repetition, and read-density bounds may depend on the requested fixed accuracies as well as the encoding construction. 1. Each seed has a validation decision whose failure probability can be made any prescribed fixed positive number. For fixed $y_s$ there is either no valid reference or a single fixed vertex $u_s$ such that, off the validation failure event, acceptance identifies $u_s$. This reference is independent of the actual random acceptance decision. It is also independent of requested confidence and numerical accuracy. If $\lVert X_s-E_u\rVert\le5\tau$, off that failure event the seed is accepted with reference $u$. Intermediate seeds with a proper reference may be accepted or rejected. An accepted seed is used only through local routines, not through a globally decoded vertex name. 2. For any accepted reference, incident-edge flags can be supplied with arbitrarily small fixed error, and bits of its own and its actual immediate neighbors’ encodings can be supplied with any prescribed fixed average error. The same bit guarantee holds for $E_{w_*}$ and the encoding of its actual successor, even if neither seed is accepted. These special words may be public or virtual. The bit guarantee is unconditioned for each fixed relevant symbolic role and branch: a request at a whole-word coordinate with density at most a fixed constant times $1/m$ has the asserted error under its given request law. It is not a guarantee conditional on selecting that branch. Requests to different word operands may use the same complete coordinate. The guarantee is required for the matching coordinate $J$ and for all preallocated statistical coordinates below. A finite union of role or fixed block-type alternatives is allowed. 3. For every finite family of bounded functions $f:[m]\to\mathbb R$ fixed by $X$, the rounded seeds’ possible actual references, and their actual candidate data, one can choose fixed sample counts so that each sample average estimates $m^{-1}\sum_jf(j)$ to any prescribed fixed additive tolerance with any prescribed fixed failure probability. The law is again unconditioned under $(I,\text{trial})$, for each fixed relevant role alternative. Every individual sampled word coordinate has uniform marginal, or the prescribed bounded-density marginal supported by the same bit-access guarantee. Corresponding word operands and physical blocks are evaluated at matching coordinates. Independent uniform samples satisfy this requirement. Other sample schemes are permitted if their concentration statement holds for the fixed underlying functions in this sense; samples and different batches need not be independent after averaging over $I$. 4. *Additional physical-read hypothesis.* After a fixed accuracy has been specified, every supplied routine has a realization with a bounded number of primitive physical read answers and bounded Boolean processing, apart from public index computations. The bound is independent of $m$. On every fixed branch of its complete physical answer tree, including branches with wrong earlier answers, the unconditioned marginal of each raw address in a physical domain of size $M$ is at most $C/M$, with a fixed $C$. A branch that uses public data need not make a physical read. These bounds hold uniformly in admissible offsets, whose refinement changes comparison constants and not address primitives or numbers of hidden-answer slots. On each fixed symbolic answer branch, the address rule itself is independent of the numerical values of these offsets.
- **Duplicated-payload encoder** ([source](#oc:encoder)): For $v:\Gamma\to U$, give every systematic cell in part $(0,0)$ the same value $v(k)$. Its full extension is denoted $$\label{oc:encoder} E_{\alpha,\beta}v,$$ or $Ev$ when its type is specified. We call this the *duplicated-payload* encoder.
- **Packed and part Hamming metrics** ([source](#oc:packing-metric)): Write $\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_V$ for relative Hamming distance on the four-part vertex set $V$. When all four parts at the same $k$ are packed into one symbol, write $\mathop{\mathrm{dist}}_\Gamma$.
- **Inner point-product bit** ([source](#ib:product-bit)): For the two contracted symbols the bit is $$Q\bigl(\pi(b_1Y_1),\pi(b_2Y_2)\bigr). \label{ib:product-bit}$$
- **Structurally canonical binary word** ([source](#ib:average-correction-section)): Call a binary word *structurally canonical* if it is obtained from the canonical recipes of Lemma <a href="#lem:inner-algebra-interface" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:inner-algebra-interface">55</a> at a specified frame, mode, progress, and arbitrary Boolean tape, followed by the point, line, row-extension, product, and repetition constructions above.
- **Fixed dummy port** ([source](#ig:port-definition)): Define $$\label{ig:port-definition} \mathcal D(s)=\bigl(\mathcal W_{\rm dum}(a_s), \mathcal W_{\rm dum}(a_s^+)\bigr), \qquad S_0=2m_{\rm dum}.$$
- **Normalized block norm** ([source](#geo:norm)): On any number of blocks of length $m$ use the inner product and norm $$\label{geo:norm} \langle U,V\rangle_{\rm b}=m^{-1}\sum_j U_jV_j, \qquad \lVert U\rVert_{\rm b}^2=m^{-1}\sum_j U_j^2.$$
- **Desired geometric endpoint set** ([source](#geo:curves)): Let $\mathcal L$ be the resulting compact union and set $$\label{geo:endpoint-set} \mathcal E=\{\text{unmatched endpoints of }\mathcal L\} \setminus\{(H_*,2)\}.$$

          "anchor": "ig:extraction-loss",
          "exact_quote": "It remains to account for adversarial concentration on designated outputs. Among all $G_0$ replica indices, discard those in the first block with mean discrepancy at least $1/4$ from the corresponding sink bit, and those with replica deviation greater than $1/8$. The squared bounds just proved and <a href=\"#ig:coarse-sync\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"ig:coarse-sync\">[ig:coarse-sync]</a> bound their respective counts, with harmless slack for normalization, by $$16(10\\tau)^2G_0\\quad\\text{and}\\quad64d_{\\rm sync}^2G_0.$$ At each remaining selected position, the physical replica differs by less than $3/8$ from the bit $f(s)$, so its distance from the physical threshold $1/2$ is greater than $1/8$. In $x$ coordinates the gap is greater than $1/24$. Since $\\varepsilon\\le\\varepsilon_g<1/100$, a satisfied extraction pair returns the correct near-bit. Every extraction pair has its own two gates, so at most $\\delta_gG_0$ designated outputs are charged for their own failed gates, even if every failed gate is concentrated there. By <a href=\"#ig:gate-count\" data-reference-type=\"eqref\" data-reference=\"ig:gate-count\">[ig:gate-count]</a>, the incorrect fraction is at most $$\\label{ig:extraction-loss}\n \\frac{16(10\\tau)^2+64d_{\\rm sync}^2+\\delta_g}{c_{\\rm sel}}\n <\\upsilon.$$ The choice of $\\tau$, synchronization radius, and failure budget reserved this divisor explicitly.",

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **invariant-centered-dilation-projection**: For a polynomial satisfying the strict degree bound, summing its pullbacks under all nonzero scalar dilations centered at the distinguished point equals its restriction to that point. The executable specialization uses a scalar polynomial over a finite field of characteristic two.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-use-degree-boundary**: Apply the projection identity when the polynomial reaches the excluded degree threshold. -> A positive homogeneous component can survive the dilation sum, so the result need not be the restriction.
- **anti-use-uncentered-dilation**: Replace the centered affine dilation by multiplication of the variable alone. -> The resulting sum projects toward a different point and does not implement the stated restriction.
- **anti-use-characteristic-transfer**: Transfer the unnormalized dilation sum unchanged to fields of a different characteristic. -> The constant homogeneous component need not have the multiplier used in the proof.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `constructive`. The dilation projection lemma is a finite algebraic construction with an explicit sum. The implementation checks its scalar specialization over finite fields of characteristic two by evaluating every field argument. Its independent oracle computes the restriction directly. Coverage is limited to this specialization and the supplied vectors; it does not certify the complete PCP reduction.

```python
# INPUTS: JSON containing modulus, generator, coeffs, and an optional test name.
# PRECONDITIONS: Irreducible binary modulus of degree 1 through 8; primitive nonzero generator; nonempty coefficients with degree strictly below q-1.
# OUTPUTS: JSON list of dilation sums, ordered by the integer representation of every field argument.
# TIME: Polynomial in field cardinality and coefficient-list length; includes exhaustive field evaluation.
# SPACE: Polynomial in field cardinality and coefficient-list length.
# ARITHMETIC: Exact characteristic-two extension-field arithmetic; symbolic irreducibility validation.
# FAILURE: Invalid inputs raise an exception and produce no accepted result.
import json
import sys
from sympy import Poly, Symbol

def require_integer(value):
    if type(value) is not int:
        raise ValueError('integer required')
    return value

def main():
    data = json.load(sys.stdin)
    modulus = require_integer(data['modulus'])
    if modulus <= 1:
        raise ValueError('invalid modulus')
    degree = modulus.bit_length() - 1
    if not 1 <= degree <= 8:
        raise ValueError('unsupported modulus degree')
    q = 1 << degree
    x = Symbol('x')
    polynomial = Poly(sum(((modulus >> j) & 1) * x**j for j in range(degree + 1)), x, modulus=2)
    if not polynomial.is_irreducible:
        raise ValueError('reducible modulus')
    generator = require_integer(data['generator'])
    coeffs = data['coeffs']
    if not isinstance(coeffs, list) or not coeffs:
        raise ValueError('nonempty coefficient list required')
    if len(coeffs) > q - 1:
        raise ValueError('strict degree bound violated')
    for coefficient in coeffs:
        if not 0 <= require_integer(coefficient) < q:
            raise ValueError('coefficient outside field')
    if not 0 < generator < q:
        raise ValueError('generator outside multiplicative group')

    def mul(a, b):
        result = 0
        while b:
            if b & 1:
                result ^= a
            b >>= 1
            a <<= 1
            if a & q:
                a ^= modulus
        return result

    seen = set()
    value = 1
    for unused in range(q - 1):
        seen.add(value)
        value = mul(value, generator)
    if value != 1 or len(seen) != q - 1:
        raise ValueError('generator is not primitive')

    def evaluate(coefficients, argument):
        value = 0
        for coefficient in reversed(coefficients):
            value = mul(value, argument) ^ coefficient
        return value

    output = []
    for z in range(q):
        total = 0
        power = 1
        for exponent in range(q - 1):
            arg = 1 ^ mul(power, z ^ 1)
            total ^= evaluate(coeffs, arg)
            power = mul(power, generator)
        output.append(total)
    print(json.dumps(output, separators=(',', ':')))

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
```

| domain | applies | strength | maturity | basis | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| software | True | strong | adaptable | inferred | The deterministic reduction constructs an explicit generalized circuit from an End-of-Line instance and decodes every acceptable rational assignment. This supplies a construction contract for a reduction compiler and its solution decoder. |
| games_simulation | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | The game reductions construct explicitly encoded equilibrium-search instances and provide solution decoders. They support hardness benchmarks for stationary policy search under the supplied initial distribution. |
| tools | True | strong | adaptable | inferred | The generalized-circuit definition gives explicit arithmetic relations and comparison and Boolean implications. These define a concrete rational assignment checker that reports failed gates and tests the acceptable-assignment contract. |
| algorithms | True | strong | adaptable | inferred | The outer uncertainty corrector is a total deterministic local map with an explicit support-containment guarantee. Its proof constructs the local decoder by enumerating label subsets, solving scalar constraints, verifying joint agreement, and applying a fixed default when decoding fails. |
| data_structures | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | The binary representation constructs balanced point, line, and compatible product blocks. Original indices and repetition copies have distinct roles, giving a concrete representation contract for encoded polynomial arrays and their query interfaces. |
| hardware_accelerators | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The constructed circuits specify approximate arithmetic and logical constraints on assignments. A physical accelerator architecture, execution model, or hardware fault-recovery implementation is ABSENT. |
| crypto_security | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The port construction supplies distance, testing, and correction guarantees. A cryptographic authentication construction, secrecy property, or computational security assumption is ABSENT. |
| machine_learning | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | The stationary-game consequences constrain equilibrium policy search, but a learning algorithm, training objective, sample-complexity guarantee, or model-estimation construction is ABSENT. |
| optimisation_operations_research | True | moderate | adaptable | inferred | The market reduction constructs equilibrium-search instances with explicit affordability, utility, and clearing conditions. It supports benchmark generation and solution decoding for the stated market family. |
| distributed_systems | False | none | not_applicable | inferred | Replica synchronization is proved for a stochastic operator acting on circuit-assignment coordinates. A message-passing protocol, distributed failure detector, or asynchronous consensus construction is ABSENT. |
| other (Coding theory and local verification) | True | strong | adaptable | inferred | The outer construction provides simultaneous systematic encoders with commuting axis extensions, injective duplicated payloads, and joint-tuple proximity guarantees. These are concrete finite coding and verification constructions. |

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **limit-fixed-parameter-regime** (formal_scope): The reduction fixes its tolerances, constants, polynomials, and algorithms independently of the input. It does not supply a uniform construction for arbitrary input-dependent accuracy choices. Blocked use: ['Treating the theorem as an approximation scheme with freely varying tolerance.', 'Replacing the fixed reduction parameters by user-selected values without rechecking the proof.']
- **limit-explicit-source-promises** (hypothesis): The source relation requires explicitly listed acyclic Boolean circuits and the stated distinguished-source promises. Blocked use: ['Applying endpoint decoding to arbitrary predecessor and successor circuits without verifying the source promises.', 'Counting only circuit gates while omitting connection and input or output descriptions.']
- **limit-global-node-consistency** (hypothesis): Failed gates may violate their relations arbitrarily, but node values remain globally consistent and inside the prescribed interval. Blocked use: ['Assigning different values to different occurrences of the same node.', 'Interpreting arbitrary failed gates as permission to change the node-value domain.']
- **limit-threshold-conventions** (edge_case): Comparison antecedents are strict, Boolean antecedents are weak, and every applicable implication must hold. Blocked use: ['Changing equality behavior at comparison boundaries.', 'Checking only a selected applicable Boolean implication.']
- **limit-boolean-tolerance-nonmonotonicity** (hypothesis): Increasing numerical tolerance can activate Boolean antecedents, so satisfied Boolean gates cannot automatically be reclassified at a larger tolerance. Blocked use: ['Relaxing Boolean tolerance monotonically.', 'Reducing tolerance through application interfaces before performing the stated Boolean-gate conversion.']
- **limit-rational-computational-decoding** (formal_scope): The soundness argument permits real assignments, but the finite search relation and computational decoder use rational assignments and account for their total encoding length. Blocked use: ['Claiming a finite polynomial-time decoder for arbitrary real-number presentations.', 'Ignoring assignment bit length when reporting decoder cost.']
- **limit-succinct-macrograph** (formal_scope): Macrograph construction bounds concern its specification and individual labels, rather than enumeration of all vertices. Blocked use: ['Treating the implicit graph as an explicitly listed graph of polynomial size.', 'Enumerating every macrovertex as a required construction stage.']
- **limit-local-code-minors** (hypothesis): The local distance and tensor-agreement guarantees require the specified scalar check-matrix minor conditions. Blocked use: ['Substituting arbitrary parity checks while retaining the same distance guarantee.', 'Using the systematic encoder before verifying the required invertibility.']
- **limit-proximity-repair-not-efficient-search** (nonconstructive): The decreasing-conflict repair establishes existence and termination without asserting efficient search through the replacement alphabet. Blocked use: ['Implementing the existential repair as though a polynomial-time replacement search had been supplied.', 'Using full-code proximity alone as the global correction algorithm.']
- **limit-duplication-separate-from-full-proximity** (hypothesis): Local validity and edge agreement do not alone establish duplicated systematic payloads; duplication requires its separate checks and exact gap. Blocked use: ['Omitting duplicated-payload comparisons from the packed tester.', 'Identifying every exact full local-and-edge word with a duplicated-payload encoding.']
- **limit-outer-correction-density-and-consistency** (hypothesis): Outer support contraction requires the stated small initial uncertainty density. Separate dependency cones may choose different uncertain values, but repeated positions must remain consistent within each cone. Blocked use: ['Claiming contraction from arbitrary initial corruption density.', 'Giving inconsistent initial values to repeated occurrences within a correction cone.']
- **limit-shared-axis-full-operations** (hypothesis): A certified full operation must satisfy the specified duplicated-payload and shared-axis conditions on arbitrary exact duplicated parents. Blocked use: ['Certifying an arbitrary local expression by isolated systematic-cell comparisons.', 'Assuming an unfinished A-only certificate also satisfies the target B constraints.']
- **limit-triangular-scratch-restoration** (hypothesis): Simultaneous scratch restoration requires triangular recurrences, correctly ordered public focus, A-coded references, and sufficiently small joint rejection. Blocked use: ['Applying the restoration estimate to cyclic scratch dependencies.', 'Using table-dependent coefficients before their public address focus is certified.']
- **limit-filling-fixed-parents** (hypothesis): Reversible full-target filling keeps its parents and coefficient data fixed throughout the schedule. Blocked use: ['Changing a parent during target preparation while retaining the advertised target identity.', 'Discarding the completed old certificate before the next target and increment are prepared.']
- **limit-finite-difference-recipes** (hypothesis): Finite-difference closure includes verification intermediates and relies on strictly decreasing assigned logical degree. Its recipes are defined independently of final tape validity. Blocked use: ['Updating only primary data while leaving retained certificates unchanged.', 'Inferring validity of an edited tape merely because its increment recipe is defined.']
- **limit-port-choice-order** (hypothesis): The encoding and port radius are chosen before actual arity, function-size factor, and output loss. Actual gadgets have additional cutoffs and require near-port inputs, gate-failure budgets, and physical-read margins. Blocked use: ['Using a gadget below its actual-gadget cutoff.', 'Dropping the near-port or spoiled-comparison premise.', 'Allowing later correction choices to silently redefine the fixed port radius.']
- **limit-average-not-pointwise-correction** (approximation): Binary correction supplies arbitrary fixed average accuracy under bounded-density requests, rather than arbitrary accuracy at every prescribed outer index. Blocked use: ['Concentrating requests at an arbitrary difficult coordinate and claiming the same correction accuracy.', 'Conditioning the error guarantee on selection of a rare branch.']
- **limit-product-joint-density** (hypothesis): Product-block requests require a joint density bound on both complete operand indices, even when the operand types agree. Blocked use: ['Replacing a product request by a diagonal pair.', 'Checking only separate point marginals while ignoring row indices or joint dependence.']
- **limit-unconditioned-complete-branch-loads** (hypothesis): Read-density bounds apply to potential slots under the original unconditioned law, including wrong, default, and unexecuted branches. Blocked use: ['Renormalizing a read law after branch selection.', 'Routing only reads observed on successful executions.', 'Broadcasting one rounded comparison result across separately charged occurrences.']
- **limit-native-tests-versus-encoded-evolution** (formal_scope): Native verification maps need not be affine over the common target field. Encoded neighbor evolution uses its separately established affine-pull interface. Blocked use: ['Propagating parity rows through arbitrary native coordinate packing.', 'Recomputing native division or coefficient extraction as though it were an allowed encoded update.']
- **limit-degree-promised-algebraic-validation** (hypothesis): The exact algebraic rejection gap is asserted for genuine polynomials within the prescribed degree bound. Blocked use: ['Applying the exact algebraic validator directly to arbitrary tables without the binary replacement argument.', 'Removing polynomial degree checks from the validity promise.']
- **limit-dilation-degree-and-characteristic** (hypothesis): The unnormalized dilation projection uses the strict coordinate-degree bound and the characteristic assumption in its proof. Blocked use: ['Including the excluded homogeneous degree.', 'Transferring the same unnormalized sum unchanged to another characteristic.', 'Replacing centered affine dilations by uncentered multiplication.']
- **limit-geometric-graph-and-tube** (hypothesis): Encoded-path geometry requires separated encodings, the stated directed incidence restrictions, and a source with an actual successor. Projection and strong-excess conclusions are local and exclude the specified endpoint neighborhoods. Blocked use: ['Applying the geometric conclusions to intersecting arbitrary graph embeddings.', 'Claiming global unique projection onto the rounded paths.', 'Extending the continuity claim across desired endpoints.']
- **limit-oracle-versus-physical-access** (hypothesis): The geometric oracle contract alone does not bound the fully expanded physical reads of substituted oracle implementations. That conclusion requires the additional physical-read hypothesis. Blocked use: ['Treating a completed Boolean oracle answer as a bounded physical circuit without an implementation argument.', 'Applying the physical-read conclusion directly to the expanded outer gadgets.']
- **limit-clipping-inside-contraction** (hypothesis): The clipped-mean estimate requires the stochastic replica contraction and an increment constant across replicas of each component. Its proof retains clipping inside the argument. Blocked use: ['Exchanging clipping with averaging.', 'Applying the same estimate to independently varying replica increments without a new bound.']
- **limit-totality-existential-witness** (nonconstructive): Rational-mesh totality follows by rounding an existential continuous fixed point; efficient computation of that fixed point is not asserted. Blocked use: ['Presenting the totality proof as a polynomial-time assignment solver.', 'Treating existence of short witnesses as an algorithm for finding them.']
- **limit-equilibrium-incentive-convention** (formal_scope): The stationary-game consequences use normalized discounted incentives evaluated from the supplied initial distribution, rather than requiring the same bound at every state. Blocked use: ['Claiming the stated hardness relation already imposes statewise incentives.', 'Dropping the initial-law restrictions of the single-controller construction.']
- **limit-game-family-transfer** (formal_scope): The stationary-game hardness statements have distinct payoff, player, action, transition, and discount restrictions. The triangular zero-sum result does not establish the corresponding claim for arbitrary zero-sum game families. <a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We prove the quasilinear-size PCP-for-PPAD conjecture of Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein. There are fixed positive rational constants <i>ε</i> and <i>δ</i> and a deterministic polynomial-time reduction that transforms an End-of-Line instance of binary length <i>N</i> into a generalized circuit of total binary length $`N(\log N)^{O(1)}`$. From any rational assignment of polynomial encoding length that <i>ε</i>-satisfies all but a <i>δ</i> fraction of the gates, a solution to the original End-of-Line instance can be recovered in polynomial time, regardless of which gates fail. Such assignments always exist, with one fixed polynomial bound on their encoding length.

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
### Introduction and the exact search relation

The class PPAD organizes total search problems whose existence proofs are based on the parity of endpoints in a directed graph (Papadimitriou 1994) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[Papadimitriou1994](#ref-Papadimitriou1994)]. Its canonical problem, End-of-Line, asks for an endpoint other than a specified source, when the graph is described by predecessor and successor circuits. Generalized circuits provide another useful language for this class: a solution assigns real values in $[0,1]$ to wires and approximately satisfies local arithmetic, comparison, and Boolean constraints. The generalized-circuit intermediary was developed by Chen, Deng, and Teng (Chen, Deng, and Teng 2007, sec. 4.2) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[CDT2007Preprint](#ref-CDT2007Preprint)]; arithmetic, comparison, and Boolean gadgets also underlie the equilibrium reductions of Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou (Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou 2009, sec. 5.1) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[DGP2009](#ref-DGP2009)]. Rubinstein established constant-error hardness with every gate required to be satisfied (Rubinstein 2018, Theorem 2) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[Rubinstein2018](#ref-Rubinstein2018)]. These results motivate the circuit language used here, with the precise normalization and thresholds specified below.

Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein formulated the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture as a quasilinear reduction from End-of-Line to generalized circuits in which both the allowed numerical error and the allowed fraction of violated gates are positive constants (Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein 2016, Conjecture 2) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[BPR2016](#ref-BPR2016)]. The failure fraction is the essential robustness requirement: the decoder must succeed even if an adversary chooses which constraints to violate. The quasilinear size requirement is a separate restriction on the reduction. Ordinary polynomial-time PPAD-hardness, even with constant numerical error, does not provide it. For example, hardness for every numerical error below $1/10$ is known for the standard generalized-circuit problem with every gate required to be satisfied (Deligkas et al. 2024, Theorem 4.1) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[DFHM2024](#ref-DFHM2024)]. Subsequent uses of PCP-for-PPAD also consider the weaker conjecture asserting ordinary PPAD-hardness with a positive failure fraction; the distinction from the original quasilinear formulation is explicit in (Deligkas et al. 2026, sec. 2.2.2) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[Fisher2026](#ref-Fisher2026)].

Rubinstein’s 2016 work combined encoded-path geometry, a locally evolving version of End-of-Line, and a holographic proof system whose certificates can be constructed and decoded through restricted access (Rubinstein 2016, secs. 3, 5, and 6) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[Rubinstein2016Settling](#ref-Rubinstein2016Settling)]. It established quasipolynomial hardness for constant-error two-player Nash under the exponential-time hypothesis for PPAD, while leaving the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture open and identifying composition as a remaining question (Rubinstein 2016, Theorem 1.2 and Section 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[Rubinstein2016Settling](#ref-Rubinstein2016Settling)]. More recently, Golowich derives sharper two-player Nash lower bounds for vanishing approximation error under PCP for PPAD together with the exponential-time hypothesis for PPAD (Golowich 2026, Theorem 1.1) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[Golowich2026](#ref-Golowich2026)]. These time lower bounds retain their additional exponential-time hypothesis; the result here concerns the conjectured reduction itself.

We give a positive resolution of the quasilinear PCP-for-PPAD conjecture. Our size bound counts the complete finite output, including connection indices, every auxiliary gate, and the bits of all rational parameters. The gate conventions below are the standard bounded-rational conventions of (Deligkas et al. 2024, 2026) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[DFHM2024](#ref-DFHM2024), [Fisher2026](#ref-Fisher2026)]; the totality and witness-size statement is proved explicitly. When restricted to the nearly linear predecessor and successor circuits in the original formulation, the theorem gives the conjectured quasilinear reduction there as well.[^1]

<a id="pm-h-3"></a>
#### The source and target problems

We fix conventional explicit binary encodings of circuit gate lists, connection indices, input and output lists, and rational parameters. Integers are encoded in binary with delimiters. All size bounds concern these complete encodings. Changing between the usual such explicit encodings changes only constant or logarithmic factors.

<a id="stmt-def-eol"></a>
<div id="def:eol" class="definition">

**Definition 1** (End-of-Line). An instance $I$ consists of two explicitly listed, acyclic, bounded-fanin Boolean circuits $$S,P:\{0,1\}^n\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^n,\qquad n\geq1,$$ using AND, OR, and NOT gates, with unrestricted fan-out, and satisfying $$P(0^n)=0^n,\qquad S(0^n)\ne0^n,\qquad P(S(0^n))=0^n.$$ A solution is a string $v\ne0^n$ such that <a id="eq:end-of-line-solution"></a>$$\label{eq:end-of-line-solution}
 P(S(v))\ne v\quad\text{or}\quad S(P(v))\ne v.$$ The input length $N\geq2$ includes the complete descriptions of both circuits and their input and output lists.

</div>

<a id="stmt-def-gcircuit"></a>
<div id="def:gcircuit" class="definition">

**Definition 2** (Generalized circuit). A generalized circuit $G=(V,T)$ has an explicitly listed finite set of nodes $V$ and a nonempty set of gates $T$. Each gate has one output and at most two inputs. A node is the output of at most one gate. Directed cycles and unrestricted fan-out are permitted. Every gate parameter $\alpha$ is a binary-encoded rational in $[0,1]$.

For an assignment $x:V\to[0,1]$, write $x_a,x_b$ for input values and $x_z$ for the output. The five arithmetic gate types are $\varepsilon$-satisfied when the corresponding condition holds: $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathrm{Constant}(\alpha;z)&:&\quad \lvert x_z-\alpha\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\
 \mathrm{Scale}(\alpha;a;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\alpha x_a\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\
 \mathrm{Copy}(a;z)&:& \lvert x_z-x_a\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\
 \mathrm{Add}(a,b;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\min\{x_a+x_b,1\}\rvert&\leq\varepsilon,\\
 \mathrm{Subtract}(a,b;z)&:& \lvert x_z-\max\{x_a-x_b,0\}\rvert&\leq\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}$$ The comparison gate $\mathrm{Less}(a,b;z)$ has the two implications $$x_a<x_b-\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,
 \qquad
 x_a>x_b+\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ x_z\leq\varepsilon.$$ The Boolean gates have the following implications: $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathrm{Or}(a,b;z):\qquad
 (x_a\geq1-\varepsilon\ \text{or}\ x_b\geq1-\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\
 (x_a\leq\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ x_b\leq\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon;\\[2pt]
 \mathrm{And}(a,b;z):\qquad
 (x_a\geq1-\varepsilon\ \text{and}\ x_b\geq1-\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\
 (x_a\leq\varepsilon\ \text{or}\ x_b\leq\varepsilon)&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon;\\[2pt]
 \mathrm{Not}(a;z):\qquad
 x_a\leq\varepsilon&\Longrightarrow x_z\geq1-\varepsilon,\\
 x_a\geq1-\varepsilon&\Longrightarrow x_z\leq\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}$$ For these four gate types, every applicable implication must hold. If no antecedent holds, any output in $[0,1]$ is permitted. In particular, the comparison thresholds are strict and the Boolean thresholds are weak.

Let $M$ be the complete binary encoding length of $G$. For fixed $\varepsilon,\delta>0$ and a fixed polynomial $p$, an acceptable assignment is rational, has total binary encoding length at most $p(M)$, and $\varepsilon$-satisfies at least $(1-\delta)|T|$ gates. Each gate has equal weight; at most $\lfloor\delta|T|\rfloor$ gates may fail. Failed gates may violate their relations arbitrarily, but all their nodes still have one globally consistent value in $[0,1]$.

</div>

The Boolean predicates make the error parameter nonmonotone: increasing $\varepsilon$ can activate an antecedent that was previously vacuous. This issue is analyzed by Schuldenzucker and Seuken (Schuldenzucker and Seuken 2019, Proposition 1) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[SchuldenzuckerSeuken2019](#ref-SchuldenzuckerSeuken2019)]. Our gate arguments use one actual tolerance throughout. Later upper bounds on that tolerance ensure explicit margins; they do not reclassify a satisfied Boolean gate at a larger tolerance.

<a id="pm-h-4"></a>
#### Main theorem

<div class="samepage">

<a id="stmt-thm-main"></a>
<div id="thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 3** (Quasilinear PCP for PPAD). *There are fixed rational constants $$0<\varepsilon<\tfrac1{10},\qquad 0<\delta<1,$$ a fixed positive integer $A$, a fixed nonnegative integer $b$, a fixed polynomial $p$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, and deterministic algorithms $R,D$ with the following properties.*

1.  *Every generalized circuit in Definition <a href="#def:gcircuit" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:gcircuit">2</a> has an acceptable rational assignment of encoding length at most $p(M)$.*

2.  *For every End-of-Line instance $I$ of length $N$, the output $R(I)$ is a generalized circuit whose complete encoding length satisfies $$M\leq A N\bigl\lceil\log_2(N+2)\bigr\rceil^b.$$*

3.  *The construction $R$ runs in time polynomial in $N$, with one fixed polynomial bound.*

4.  *For every acceptable assignment $x$ of $R(I)$, the algorithm $D(I,x)$ returns a solution of $I$ in time polynomial in $N$ plus the encoding length of $x$, with one fixed polynomial bound.*

*All constants, polynomials, and algorithms are chosen once. They use no advice depending on the input length and no randomized construction.*

</div>

</div>

The conclusion about $D$ is universal over the locations and values of the failed gates. In fact, the soundness argument applies to arbitrary real assignments meeting the gate-failure budget; rationality is needed for the finite search relation and its computational decoder. The totality proof supplies an assignment satisfying every gate on a fixed rational mesh. Neither tolerance tends to zero with $N$.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
#### Proof strategy: encoded paths and robust local computation

We begin with the geometric target of the reduction. Replace the End-of-Line graph by a locally evolving directed graph with a known source, no isolated vertices, and the same endpoint-decoding property. Represent each vertex $w$ by a separated binary word $E_w\in\{0,1\}^m$. In the box $[-1,2]^{4m}$, viewed as four blocks of $m$ coordinates, each edge $u\to v$ traces a polygon that first changes a copy of $E_u$ to $E_v$, changes a repeated control bit, updates the other copy, and resets the control bit. Rounded corners join these polygons into paths and cycles. An additional segment enters the known source, and a separate field prescription handles its far end. Every other path endpoint encodes an End-of-Line answer.

Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">10</a> constructs a bounded displacement field $v$ on this box. Close to a path it uses the directed tangent and the inward normal; farther away it passes to a fixed direction. For a sufficiently small fixed step $\beta>0$, the clipped move $\mathop{\mathrm{clip}}(X+\beta v(X))-X$ has norm at least a fixed positive multiple of $\beta$ outside a fixed neighborhood of the desired endpoints. Here clipping keeps each coordinate in the box, and the norm is normalized by the word length. Thus an accurate enough approximate fixed point identifies an endpoint. The proof must also provide local numerical access to the field: it cannot inspect the entire encoded graph when computing one coordinate of $v$.

This use of encoded paths and restricted access has a close predecessor in Rubinstein’s holographic proof system (Rubinstein 2016, secs. 3, 5, and 6) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[Rubinstein2016Settling](#ref-Rubinstein2016Settling)]. The present reduction needs two further properties simultaneously: quasilinear total storage and robustness to an arbitrary fixed fraction of failed gates. The two scales of the construction address these requirements as follows.

**A quasilinear outer word.** Sections <a href="#sec:macrograph" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:macrograph">2</a>–<a href="#sec:outer-representation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-representation">5</a> construct canonical representations $$R_w=(s_k)_{k\in\Gamma},\qquad
 s_k\in\{0,1\}^L,\qquad
 |\Gamma|=N(\log N)^{O(1)},\qquad L=(\log N)^{O(1)}.$$ A bounded number of symbol positions suffices to test local validity, propose a neighboring symbol, or perform one correction step. Each such operation has Boolean complexity polynomial in $L$, with an exponent fixed before the later correction accuracy. Distinct valid words have constant symbol distance, and a word within a fixed symbol-error radius can be decoded globally in polynomial time.

Begin with the sparse transcript graph of Section <a href="#sec:macrograph" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:macrograph">2</a>, whose vertices record partial computations of the predecessor and successor circuits and whose edges change one tape position and its occupation bit. Transcript validity is expressed by bounded-degree polynomial equations in the tape entries. Sampling an individual equation could miss one false equation. Sections <a href="#sec:outer-codes" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-codes">3</a> and <a href="#sec:outer-programs" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-programs">4</a> instead encode polynomial remainders recording the equation residuals, and retain certificates for the intermediate products and linear computations that produce them. On exact codewords, a nonzero remainder differs from zero at a constant fraction of positions. The code’s commuting row and column constraints also permit whole-row or whole-column comparisons that give a constant gap for an incorrect certificate identity. All stored components are tested together on one fixed list of neighboring positions, so more certificates enlarge a symbol without diluting the gap.

One tape edit can change all these encoded arrays. Before making an allowed edit, Section <a href="#sec:outer-representation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-representation">5</a> prepares each retained array’s finite difference: its value on the edited tape minus its value on the old tape. Certificates introduced by this preparation need their own increments as well. Each new increment has lower assigned polynomial degree in the logical tape entries, so this recursion has bounded depth. Once preparation is complete, adding the increments updates the whole retained tuple to its canonical value on the new tape; the preparation can then be reversed.

The remaining storage issue is the long linear computation needed to prepare an increment. It is carried out one small group of Fourier frequencies at a time: each such orbit is preserved by the encoder and has only polylogarithmically many frequencies. A clock records progress and scratch space is reused. Thus the preparation’s elapsed time lengthens the represented path rather than the data stored at a vertex. The resulting words are the locally evolving $R_w$ above.

**One fixed binary port.** A polynomial-size robust construction applied directly to an $N$-bit vertex would not give the required size. Instead we apply it only to the $L$-bit outer symbols. The inner construction supplies one injective encoding $$\mathcal D:\{0,1\}^L\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{S_0},
 \qquad S_0=\operatorname{poly}(L),
 \qquad E_w=(\mathcal D(s_k))_{k\in\Gamma}.$$ Its encoding and positive correction radius are chosen before the number of symbols inspected by a local function. From that fixed radius, it supports every prescribed fixed average accuracy for requests with bounded address density. More outer correction rounds may enlarge the number of symbols inspected, and hence the number of input ports in the resulting local computation. More inner correction rounds improve its requested bit accuracy. These choices may enlarge constant factors, but they do not change $\mathcal D$ or its radius. All polynomial factors in $L$ remain fixed powers of $\log N$.

Sections <a href="#sec:inner-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:inner-algebra">7</a>–<a href="#sec:inner-gadget" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:inner-gadget">9</a> construct this port and its robust decision gadget independently of the outer reduction. For a fixed tuple $s=(s_1,\ldots,s_k)$ of $L$-bit inputs to a Boolean function $f$, the inner graph is one computation path with blank work at its source and output $f(s)$ at its sink. Polynomial charts encode its tapes and certificates. Their dependencies are kept separate for each read-only input, including throughout the finite-difference closure. Consequently the input-dependent parts of the source and its first successor have the same formulas in every later invocation. A one-input template at these two labels defines $\mathcal D(s_i)$ for one input $s_i$; its bits then supply the source data for an actual multi-input computation.

The binary representation in Section <a href="#sec:inner-binary" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:inner-binary">8</a> adds point tables, line tables, and tables for the required products. Correction keeps both addresses in each product request and preserves the required bound on their joint distribution. Its error bound is averaged over requested coordinates; arbitrarily accurate correction at every individual coordinate is neither asserted nor needed. At the inner scale, the geometric construction forces a feedback state near the unique sink, where a positive fraction of encoded coordinates reveal $f(s)$. These become the many designated outputs of the decision gadget.

**From local decisions to an endpoint under gate failures.** Section <a href="#sec:outer-composition" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-composition">6</a> uses the outer tester and correction routines to supply the field’s local information. Two rounded blocks serve as possible vertex encodings. On good validation decisions, each accepted seed has a unique reference vertex; corrected calls supply its incident flags and the requested bits of its own and neighboring encodings. The geometric estimator reserves a bounded list of possible pieces and estimates their statistics before selecting a numerical winner. This order makes average bit accuracy sufficient even when the selected piece depends on the output coordinate.

The generalized circuit has many physical replicas of each geometric coordinate. Write $X_{ir}$ for replica $r$ of component $i$, and $\bar X_i$ for their mean. A fixed-degree expander average $A$ couples the replicas. Each output is produced by a circuit that realizes the approximate relation $$X_{ir}\approx\mathop{\mathrm{clip}}\bigl((AX)_{ir}
                       +\beta\widehat v_{ir}(\bar X)\bigr),$$ where $\widehat v$ is the bounded local field estimator. First, boundedness of the update and the expander gap force the replicas close to their means, without assuming that any decision is correct. This synchronization then bounds the number of reads far from their means. Randomized threshold offsets control ambiguous comparisons, and the gate-failure budget controls the circuits containing a failed gate. The randomness describes the sampling analysis: the printed circuit assigns replicas a deterministically enumerated list of fixed tapes of size polynomial in $L$.

These charges apply to the complete wired computation. All hypothetical answer branches are allocated before routing, and each physical read occurrence is routed separately with bounded load. Expensive Boolean decision gadgets are shared by groups of output replicas. Their many designated outputs ensure that failures concentrated on extraction wires still spoil only a controlled fraction of the group. On reliable outputs the update approximates the true field; on unreliable outputs whose gates are satisfied, its bounded size still gives an error proportional to $\beta$, apart from the numerical gate tolerance. An estimate that keeps clipping inside the replica contraction argument then makes the mean an approximate fixed point. The displacement lower bound forces $\bar X$ near an endpoint. Rounding its first block and applying the global binary and outer decoders yields the required End-of-Line answer.

The same synchronization, error charging, and clipped-mean argument is used inside the decision gadget. At that scale every output has its own bounded estimator circuit; the additional sharing of decision gadgets occurs only in the outer composition. In both uses, a fixed hypothetical answer branch is analyzed under the original random-tape law, rather than by conditioning on that branch being executed.

**Organization and imported inputs.** Section <a href="#sec:outer-composition" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:outer-composition">6</a> assembles the main theorem from the outer representation, the port interface stated there, and the independent geometric interface. It proves universal decoding, the complete binary size bound, and rational-witness totality. Sections <a href="#sec:inner-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:inner-algebra">7</a>–<a href="#sec:inner-gadget" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:inner-gadget">9</a> prove the port interface, and Section <a href="#sec:geometry" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:geometry">10</a> proves both the displacement bound and finite numerical access. Section <a href="#sec:weak-nash" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:weak-nash">11</a> gives the consequences described below. Appendix <a href="#sec:extensions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:extensions">12</a> collects the separate full-macrograph and unrestricted-product variants; these are not prerequisites for the fixed-port composition.

The outer code uses ternary Goldbach, fixed-generator prime-quotient expansion, and an effective least-prime bound (Helfgott 2013; Bourgain and Gamburd 2008; Xylouris 2009) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[Helfgott2013](#ref-Helfgott2013), [BG2008](#ref-BG2008), [Xylouris2011](#ref-Xylouris2011)]. Its simultaneous systematic encoders, matrix twists, and joint correction guarantees are proved here; a general locally testable code theorem such as (Dinur et al. 2022) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[DEL+2022](#ref-DEL+2022)] does not by itself supply this combination. The inner binary construction uses the corrected scalar line test and two group-theoretic inputs (Friedl and Sudan 2013; Ershov and Jaikin-Zapirain 2010; Shalom 1999) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[FS1995](#ref-FS1995), [EJZ2010](#ref-EJZ2010), [Shalom1999](#ref-Shalom1999)]; its vector replacement, affine expansion, and average correction are proved here. The all-modulus Margulis–Gabber–Galil bound supplies the local and replica walks (Karayel 2023) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[MGGAFP](#ref-MGGAFP)]. The inner fields and groups are introduced afresh and are distinct from those of the outer construction.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
#### Consequences for games and markets

Section <a href="#sec:weak-nash" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:weak-nash">11</a> applies the theorem to the conditional reductions for weak approximate Nash and relative bimatrix Nash (Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein 2016) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[BPR2016](#ref-BPR2016)], course allocation (Babichenko, Papadimitriou, and Rubinstein 2016) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[BPR2016](#ref-BPR2016)], markets with approximately optimal bundles (Deligkas et al. 2026) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[Fisher2026](#ref-Fisher2026)], stationary equilibria in discounted games (Daskalakis, Golowich, and Zhang 2023; Park, Zhang, and Ozdaglar 2023; Farina et al. 2026) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[DGZ2023](#ref-DGZ2023), [PZO2025](#ref-PZO2025), [FKPP2026](#ref-FKPP2026)], and approximate Hylland–Zeckhauser allocation (Braverman et al. 2026) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[HZ2026](#ref-HZ2026)]. For each target we state the precise approximation and encoding conventions before its consequence. The cited reductions provide the transfers to these problems. We supply the needed gate-basis and fan-out conversions, track their fixed error and failure losses, and verify the rational witness and decoder bounds. These consequences use fixed-gap circuit hardness; the quasilinear complete-output bound is the additional assertion of Theorem <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">3</a>.

<a id="sec:macrograph"></a>
### A sparse macrograph for End-of-Line

We first replace the circuit transitions by a graph in which one edge changes at most one tape bit and its occupation bit. The graph is specified by short labels and local transition rules; its vertices are not enumerated. The use of a clock to expose sparse circuit updates has a close precedent in Rubinstein’s LocalEndOfALine construction (Rubinstein 2016, secs. 5–5.1) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[Rubinstein2016Settling](#ref-Rubinstein2016Settling)], where a counter schedules activation and deactivation of individual wires. We give the transcript, reciprocal proposals, and bounded-incidence validity description needed here explicitly.

<a id="macro:promises"></a>
Throughout the outer construction, let $n_0$ be the number of input bits of the End-of-Line instance and let $N$ be its complete binary encoding length. We use the promises $$\label{macro:promises}
 P(0^{n_0})=0^{n_0},\qquad S(0^{n_0})\ne0^{n_0},\qquad
 P(S(0^{n_0}))=0^{n_0}.$$ Thus a nonzero string $y$ is an answer if <a id="macro:answer"></a>$$\label{macro:answer}
 P(S(y))\ne y\quad\hbox{or}\quad S(P(y))\ne y.$$

<a id="macro:transcripts"></a>
#### Sparse transcripts and their two orders

Normalize both circuits to gates of fan-in at most two. In particular, replace any larger AND or OR by a binary tree. Give every input and every gate a distinct tape position. For each listed output, introduce a separate terminal copy gate, even if several listed outputs originally name the same wire. Replace the outgoing uses of a wire by a binary tree of copy gates, including its uses as feeds to terminal copies. A wire with $d$ uses needs $O(d)$ such gates. The total number of positions is therefore bounded by a constant times the number of gates, connections, and input and output list entries in the original instance, and hence is $O(N)$.

These changes preserve $S$ and $P$. They also make every tape position an operand of only a bounded number of internal gate rules. Choose a topological order of the nonterminal gates of each circuit, followed by all its terminal output copies. Such an order exists because those copies have no internal consumers: any branching needed for other uses was placed before them. Copy gates here are auxiliary transcript rules and need not belong to the source circuit’s original basis.

Pad the tape with dummy positions to a power of two $h=2^\ell$. An arbitrary fixed lower cutoff on $h$ may be imposed, and still $h=O(N)$. Write $[h]=\{0,\ldots,h-1\}$. On these same positions define the two permutations $$\begin{aligned}
 \pi_{\mathrm f}:\;&S\text{ inputs},\ S\text{ gates},\
 P\text{ inputs},\ P\text{ gates},\ \text{dummies},\\
 \pi_{\mathrm r}:\;&P\text{ inputs},\ P\text{ gates},\
 S\text{ inputs},\ S\text{ gates},\ \text{dummies},
\end{aligned}$$ using the chosen gate order inside each block. For a content array $D\in\{0,1\}^{[h]}$, let $\operatorname{pref}_{\pi,k}(D)$ agree with $D$ on $\pi(0),\ldots,\pi(k-1)$ and be zero elsewhere. Its occupation array is the indicator of these $k$ positions. Empty and full tapes have occupation arrays $\mathbf 0$ and $\mathbf 1$, respectively. The content and occupation arrays are separate: an occupied position may contain zero.

For a full content array $D$, the notation $\operatorname{in}_S(D)$, $\operatorname{out}_S(D)$, $\operatorname{in}_P(D)$, and $\operatorname{out}_P(D)$ denotes the vectors at the designated input or terminal output positions. A *valid full transcript* $Q_x$ computes $S$ on input $x$, copies its output to the inputs of $P$, computes $P$, and satisfies <a id="macro:full-transcript"></a>$$\label{macro:full-transcript}
 \operatorname{in}_S(Q_x)=x,\qquad
 \operatorname{in}_P(Q_x)=\operatorname{out}_S(Q_x),\qquad
 \operatorname{out}_P(Q_x)=x.$$ Its dummy positions are zero. Consequently $Q_x$ exists precisely when $P(S(x))=x$, and is unique when it exists.

For every $y\in\{0,1\}^{n_0}$, define two complete computation templates, without imposing any terminal comparisons. The template $U_y$ first computes $S(y)$ and then $P(S(y))$; the template $V_y$ first computes $P(y)$ and then $S(P(y))$. Both occupy the same tape coordinates and have zero dummies. In $V_y$, the $P$ inputs are $y$ and the $S$ inputs are $P(y)$. Thus $U_y$ is a valid full transcript exactly when $P(S(y))=y$, in which case it is $Q_y$; and $V_y$ is a valid full transcript exactly when $S(P(y))=y$, in which case it is $Q_{P(y)}$.

<a id="stmt-macro-prefixes"></a>
<div id="macro:prefixes" class="definition">

**Definition 4** (Computed prefixes). A *forward prefix of length $k$ with parameter $y$* has the first $k$ positions in $\pi_{\mathrm f}$ occupied. At occupied positions it obeys these rules: $S$ inputs copy the corresponding bits of $y$; $P$ inputs copy the corresponding designated $S$ outputs; every gate obeys its Boolean or copy rule; and dummies are zero. In addition, each occupied designated $P$ output equals the corresponding bit of $y$. Unoccupied contents are zero.

A *reconstruction prefix of length $k$ from $y$* uses $\pi_{\mathrm r}$. Its occupied $P$ inputs copy $y$, its occupied $S$ inputs copy the designated $P$ outputs, and its occupied gates and dummies obey the same rules as above. Each occupied designated $S$ output must additionally equal the corresponding bit of $y$. Unoccupied contents are again zero.

</div>

Every operand in a prefix rule is either an earlier occupied position or a specified bit of $y$. In particular, a designated comparison is an extra test on the newly computed terminal copy, not a substitute for its computation rule.

<a id="stmt-macro-prefix-uniqueness"></a>
<div id="macro:prefix-uniqueness" class="lemma">

**Lemma 5** (Unique prefixes and their first obstruction). *For a fixed $y$, the valid forward prefixes exist uniquely for an initial interval of lengths $0\le k\le k_{\mathrm f}(y)$ and equal $\operatorname{pref}_{\pi_{\mathrm f},k}(U_y)$. The valid reconstruction prefixes likewise exist uniquely for $0\le k\le k_{\mathrm r}(y)$ and equal $\operatorname{pref}_{\pi_{\mathrm r},k}(V_y)$. Moreover, <a id="macro:forward-obstruction"></a><a id="macro:reverse-obstruction"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 k_{\mathrm f}(y)=h&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P(S(y))=y,
 \label{macro:forward-obstruction}\\
 k_{\mathrm r}(y)=h&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S(P(y))=y.
 \label{macro:reverse-obstruction}
\end{aligned}$$ If a maximal length is less than $h$, the next position is a designated output at which the additional comparison fails.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-macro-prefix-uniqueness"><summary>Proof of stmt-macro-prefix-uniqueness</summary>

*Proof.* Induct along the relevant order. Input copies, gates, and dummies uniquely determine the next content bit from data already determined. These are exactly the bits of $U_y$ or $V_y$. The only possible obstruction is an additional terminal comparison. Shortening a valid prefix removes requirements without changing retained bits, so the valid lengths form an initial interval. At length $h$, all terminal comparisons have been imposed, giving the two equivalences. ◻

</details>

<a id="macro:schedule"></a>
#### The cyclic schedule and reciprocal proposals

A logical tape vector is $$b=(A,E^A,B,E^B)\in\{0,1\}^{4h},$$ where $A,B$ are contents and $E^A,E^B$ are occupations. The schedule uses four phases. To see their effect when all computations succeed, suppose $Q_x$ and $Q_y$ exist and $y=S(x)$. Starting with $A=Q_x$ and $B$ empty, it fills $B$ with $Q_y$, erases $A$ by reversing reconstruction from $y$, copies $B$ into $A$, and erases $B$. The resulting tapes are $A=Q_y$ and $B$ empty. The identity $P(y)=x$, which follows from validity of $Q_x$, is what makes the reconstruction recover the old tape.

For intermediate prefixes, including those at a failed terminal comparison, validity is defined as follows. The stage $s$ lies in $\mathbb Z/(4h)\mathbb Z$. Write $\mathcal V_s$ for the following set of valid logical vectors; the endpoint descriptions in adjacent cases are identified.

1.  $0\le s\le h$: $A=Q_x$ is full for some $x$, and $B$ is a forward prefix of length $s$ with parameter $y=\operatorname{out}_S(A)=S(x)$.

2.  $h\le s\le2h$: $B=Q_y$ is full for some $y$, and $A$ is a reconstruction prefix of length $2h-s$ from $y=\operatorname{in}_S(B)$.

3.  $2h\le s\le3h$: $B$ is a valid full transcript and $A=\operatorname{pref}_{\pi_{\mathrm f},s-2h}(B)$. This copied prefix has no additional computation requirements.

4.  $3h\le s\le4h$: $A$ is a valid full transcript and $B=\operatorname{pref}_{\pi_{\mathrm f},4h-s}(A)$.

Occupations in every case are the stated full or prefix indicators. Stage $4h$ is stage $0$, at which $A$ is full and $B$ is empty.

<a id="stmt-macro-boundaries"></a>
<div id="macro:boundaries" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (Boundary agreement). *The two validity descriptions agree at each of $h,2h,3h$, and $4h=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-macro-boundaries"><summary>Proof of stmt-macro-boundaries</summary>

*Proof.* At stage $h$, the first description gives $$A=Q_x,\qquad B=Q_y,\qquad y=S(x),\qquad P(y)=x.$$ The reconstruction template from $y$ computes $P(y)=x$ and then $S(x)=y$, so it agrees with $A$ at every position and satisfies all its comparisons. This gives the second description. Conversely, the second description at $h$ gives $B=Q_y$ and a full reconstruction $A=V_y$ with $S(P(y))=y$. Put $x=P(y)$. Then $P(S(x))=P(y)=x$, so $A=Q_x$ and $\operatorname{out}_S(A)=y$. Since $B=Q_y$, it is the full forward prefix required in the first description. These identities include all copy gates and dummies. At $2h$, both descriptions have $A$ empty and $B$ a valid full transcript. At $3h$, both have $A=B$ a valid full transcript. At $4h=0$, both have $A$ full and $B$ empty. ◻

</details>

For each *start frame* $c\in\{0,\ldots,4h-1\}$, define a forward proposal $F_c$ from stage $c$ to stage $c+1$, and a reverse proposal $R_c$ from stage $c+1$ to stage $c$, with stages reduced modulo $4h$. Thus at current stage $s$, the successor uses $F_s$ and the predecessor uses $R_{s-1}$, where the latter subscript is reduced modulo $4h$. The following table specifies their content changes. Every fill or copy sets the corresponding occupation to one, and every erasure sets it to zero. All other bits remain unchanged.

<div class="center">

| Start frame  | Position $j$              | $F_c$               | $R_c$                        |
|:-------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------|:-----------------------------|
| $0\le c<h$   | $\pi_{\mathrm f}(c)$      | fill $B_j$ forward  | erase $B_j$                  |
| $h\le c<2h$  | $\pi_{\mathrm r}(2h-c-1)$ | erase $A_j$         | fill $A_j$ by reconstruction |
| $2h\le c<3h$ | $\pi_{\mathrm f}(c-2h)$   | copy $B_j$ to $A_j$ | erase $A_j$                  |
| $3h\le c<4h$ | $\pi_{\mathrm f}(4h-c-1)$ | erase $B_j$         | copy $A_j$ to $B_j$          |

</div>

A computed fill always writes its Boolean rule value, even if the additional terminal comparison fails. Thus the proposal itself is defined separately from the test of whether its result is valid.

The *macrograph* has vertex set $$\mathcal V=\{(s,b):s\in\mathbb Z/(4h)\mathbb Z, b\in\mathcal V_s\}.$$ It has an edge $(c,b)\longrightarrow(c+1,b')$ precisely when $b'=F_c(b)$ and both endpoints are valid.

<a id="stmt-macro-local-edges"></a>
<div id="macro:local-edges" class="lemma">

<a id="macro:reciprocity"></a>
**Lemma 7** (Reciprocity and local existence tests). *Whenever $b\in\mathcal V_c$ and $b'\in\mathcal V_{c+1}$, $$\label{macro:reciprocity}
 b'=F_c(b)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b=R_c(b').$$ For a valid input to either proposal, validity of its output is determined by a bounded number of bits at public, frame-dependent addresses. The forward proposal can fail only when $0\le c<h$ and the new forward terminal comparison fails. The reverse proposal can fail only when $h\le c<2h$ and the new reconstruction terminal comparison fails. The graph has indegree and outdegree at most one, and no self-edges.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-macro-local-edges"><summary>Proof of stmt-macro-local-edges</summary>

*Proof.* In the first range, erasing the newly filled position recovers its previous blank content and occupation. Conversely, a valid longer forward prefix has the uniquely prescribed value at its last position, so filling its shortened prefix recovers it. In the second range, erasure shortens a reconstruction prefix. Its erased value is uniquely determined by earlier retained positions and the unchanged full tape $B$, so reverse reconstruction recovers it. The converse follows from the same uniqueness. In the last two ranges, the unchanged full tape determines the copied value, and erasure recovers the blank position. Boundary agreement applies to each use of these statements at a boundary. In particular, at $c=4h-1$, the reverse proposal from stage zero copies $A_{\pi_{\mathrm f}(0)}$ into the first forward position of the empty $B$ tape, exactly reversing the wraparound erasure.

Shortening a valid computed prefix is always valid, as are extending or shortening a copied prefix. When extending a computed prefix, all earlier conditions remain true. Its next value is obtained from at most two earlier operands or a specified full-tape input bit, so the only new condition that can fail is the stated terminal comparison. That comparison needs one additional specified bit. Thus the relevant operands, old bits, and comparison bits suffice to decide both proposals and the corresponding existence flags. Equation <a href="#macro:reciprocity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="macro:reciprocity">[macro:reciprocity]</a> gives at most one predecessor, and the definition gives at most one successor. Every edge changes the stage by one modulo $4h$, and $4h\ge4$, so no edge is a self-edge. ◻

</details>

<a id="macro:interface"></a>
#### Endpoints, sparse edits, and uniform size

The following statement is the interface used by the evolving representation.

<a id="stmt-lem-macrograph"></a>
<div id="lem:macrograph" class="lemma">

**Lemma 8** (Macrograph interface). *From every promised End-of-Line instance of explicit length $N$, one can deterministically construct, in time polynomial in $N$, the above tape specification with $h=2^\ell=O(N)$, the stage conditions $\mathcal V_c$, and the following data and algorithms.*

1.  *The macrograph has indegree and outdegree at most one, no self-edges, and no isolated vertices. It has a distinguished source $v_*$ whose label and actual successor are computable in polynomial time. Every endpoint other than $v_*$ supplies a nonzero End-of-Line answer by reading a designated vector on a full tape.*

2.  *Forward and reverse proposals at the same start frame are reciprocal on valid pairs. Their edits and existence flags use only a fixed number of logical bits at public addresses, with a fixed finite set of Boolean decision rules.*

3.  *There is a fixed finite alphabet $\Sigma=\{-1,0,1\}^4$ and public edit vectors $h_\sigma(c)$ such that each chosen proposal has the form $b\mapsto b+h_\sigma(c)$. One public address is allotted to each logical array. On actual edges only the active tape’s content position and its occupation position can change. The same fixed edit formulas are defined over any field, whether or not their arguments represent valid Boolean tapes.*

4.  *For each fixed phase, the local tape requirements have bounded arity and bounded operand multiplicity, uniformly in $N$. The full tape specification and all frame-dependent rule and address tables have $O(h)$ records of $O(\log(N+2))$ bits each. A vertex label has $4h+\lceil\log_2(4h)\rceil=O(N)$ bits; validity and endpoint decoding take polynomial time. These bounds concern descriptions and individual labels and do not require enumeration of the macrograph.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-macrograph"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-macrograph</summary>

<a id="macro:sink-identity"></a>
*Proof.* We first identify all endpoints. A missing successor can occur only in the first range of the schedule. Write its full tape as $A=Q_x$ and put $y=\operatorname{out}_S(A)=S(x)$. The current $B$ tape is its longest valid forward prefix, so Lemma <a href="#macro:prefix-uniqueness" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="macro:prefix-uniqueness">5</a> gives $$\label{macro:sink-identity}
 P(S(y))\ne y,\qquad P(y)=x.$$ If $y=0^{n_0}$, then $x=P(0^{n_0})=0^{n_0}$ and $y=S(0^{n_0})\ne0^{n_0}$, a contradiction. Thus this designated vector is a nonzero End-of-Line answer. Such a vertex has a predecessor: shorten its forward prefix when its length is positive; at stage zero use the reverse wraparound copy from the preceding frame.

<a id="macro:source-identity"></a>
A missing predecessor can occur only at a stage $s=c+1$ with $h\le c<2h$. Its full tape is $B=Q_y$, where $y=\operatorname{in}_S(B)$, and its reconstruction prefix has its maximal length $k_{\mathrm r}(y)<h$. Hence $$\label{macro:source-identity}
 s=2h-k_{\mathrm r}(y),\qquad S(P(y))\ne y.$$ For $y\ne0^{n_0}$ this is again a permitted answer. The vertex has a successor obtained by shortening the reconstruction prefix; if the prefix is empty, the next copying step supplies a successor. Every proposal in the two copying ranges succeeds in the relevant direction, except that an incoming reconstruction proposal at stage $2h$ is covered by the case just considered. Together with Lemma <a href="#macro:local-edges" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="macro:local-edges">7</a>, this exhausts the possible missing neighbors and proves that no vertex is isolated.

It remains to specify the zero-labelled exception. The last promise in <a href="#macro:promises" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="macro:promises">[macro:promises]</a> supplies the unique full transcript $Q_{0^{n_0}}$, whereas the first two promises give $$S(P(0^{n_0}))=S(0^{n_0})\ne0^{n_0}.$$ Let $k_*=k_{\mathrm r}(0^{n_0})<h$. Then $v_*$ is exactly the vertex at stage $2h-k_*$ whose $B$ tape is $Q_{0^{n_0}}$ and whose $A$ tape is $\operatorname{pref}_{\pi_{\mathrm r},k_*}(V_{0^{n_0}})$, with their prescribed occupations. Prefix uniqueness proves that this is the only missing-predecessor vertex with designated vector zero. It has no predecessor and has the successor just described. Evaluate $U_{0^{n_0}}$ and $V_{0^{n_0}}$, locate the first failed reconstruction terminal comparison, and take the preceding prefix. This computes $v_*$ and its successor in polynomial time. This proves the endpoint claims, including the existence of the public source. Other directed paths and directed cycles may remain in the graph; nothing here requires one connected component.

<a id="macro:finite-edits"></a>
We next make the local edit interface explicit. At start frame $c$, let $j(c)$ be the position in the transition table. Allot this position to the content and occupation arrays of the active tape, and allot the fixed default position $0$ to the two inactive arrays. Denote these four addresses by $j_D(c)$, for $D\in\{A,E^A,B,E^B\}$. If $\mathbf e_{D,j}$ is the unit vector at position $j$ of array $D$, define, over a field $K$, $$\label{macro:finite-edits}
 h_\sigma(c)=\sum_{D\in\{A,E^A,B,E^B\}}
       \sigma_D\mathbf e_{D,j_D(c)}\in K^{4h},
 \qquad \sigma\in\{-1,0,1\}^4,$$ where the integers $-1,0,1$ are mapped into $K$. For a proposed Boolean write, choose its content coefficient as the desired bit minus the old bit and its occupation coefficient as the desired occupation minus the old occupation. Set both inactive coefficients to zero. Each coefficient lies in $\{-1,0,1\}$, and the resulting additive edit is precisely the proposal, in either direction. The vector in <a href="#macro:finite-edits" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="macro:finite-edits">[macro:finite-edits]</a> is public once $c$ and $\sigma$ are fixed; addition by it is defined on all of $K^{4h}$. The assertion about valid Boolean proposals does not require a validity interpretation for other field-valued inputs.

The necessary public data at a frame are its phase, active tape, write position, rule type, at most two operand addresses, the old content and occupation addresses, and, when applicable, the extra comparison address. A forward fill uses its forward rule; a reverse fill uses its reconstruction rule. Lemma <a href="#macro:local-edges" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="macro:local-edges">7</a> shows that the existence flag is the new comparison result in the only direction where failure is possible, and is one otherwise. These are fixed Boolean decisions once the finitely many addressed bits and public rule data are supplied. Define the decisions on arbitrary Boolean reads by the same formulas, using a fixed default rule and address for unused roles. Their agreement with graph neighbors is asserted on valid input vertices. No global validity check or full circuit evaluation is hidden in an existence flag.

For completeness, the bounded-multiplicity assertion includes more than internal gate edges. Each internal value has boundedly many uses after copy-tree normalization. Each designated output is used once by the other circuit’s input-copy rule and participates in only a bounded number of terminal or external-vector comparisons. Each external-vector bit is used once as an input bit and once for its corresponding terminal comparison. Copied-prefix equations use each full-tape position once. Occupation indicators condition only the rules at their positions; prefix monotonicity, if expressed by adjacent-position tests, reads a position at most twice in each order. Thus all local content, bitness, occupation, gate, copy, comparison, and dummy conditions use bounded-arity records, and each logical position appears as an operand only boundedly often across the fixed list of phases. The requirement that the occupied prefix have its specified length is separate: one may either inspect the prescribed occupation pattern directly, or use prefix monotonicity together with the occupation sum.
